claim: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by substantial neuronal loss in both the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by substantial neuronal loss in both the central and peripheral nervous systems (Gorman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gorman, 2008

claim: In dementia-related conditions like Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and dementia with Lewy bodies, neurodegeneration can lead to progressive damage in brain regions related with memory, behavior, and cognition.
source: In dementia-related conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), neurodegeneration can lead to progressive damage in brain regions related with memory, behavior, and cognition (Duong et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duong et al., 2017

claim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is thought to primarily affect motor neurons.
source: Other diseases are thought to primarily affect the locomotor system, including motor neurons in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and nigrostriatal dopaminergic circuitry in Parkinson's disease (PD) (Bosco et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bosco et al., 2011

claim: Parkinson's disease is thought to primarily affect nigrostriatal dopaminergic circuitry.
source: Other diseases are thought to primarily affect the locomotor system, including motor neurons in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and nigrostriatal dopaminergic circuitry in Parkinson's disease (PD) (Bosco et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bosco et al., 2011

claim: Most neurodegenerative disorders share same molecular and cellular mechanisms.
source: Although each disorder has its own distinct etiology, progression, affected brain areas, and clinical manifestations, recent studies support that most of them share same molecular and cellular mechanisms (Wingo et al., 2022; Huseby et al., 2023; Arneson et al., 2018; Zeighami et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wingo et al., 2022; Huseby et al., 2023; Arneson et al., 2018; Zeighami et al., 2023

claim: Non-neuronal cells such as astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, as well as cells of the vascular and peripheral immune systems are gaining more recognition for their contribution to disease pathology.
source: While research has been mainly focused on neuronal dysfunction, other brain cells such as astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, as well as cells of the vascular and peripheral immune systems, are gaining more recognition for their contribution to disease pathology (Bordone and Barbosa-Morais, 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Reynolds et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bordone and Barbosa-Morais, 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Reynolds et al., 2019

claim: Non-neuronal cells in the brain can play a dual role, with their complex response having both protective and detrimental effects on neuronal health and survival depending on the disease stage.
source: Depending on the disease stage, non-neuronal cells in the brain can play a dual role, with their complex response having both protective and detrimental effects on neuronal health and survival (Geloso et al., 2017; Jiwaji et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geloso et al., 2017; Jiwaji et al., 2022

claim: Astrocytes and microglia are involved in neuronal support, maintenance of extracellular homeostasis, and immune regulation in response to injury.
source: For instance, such glial cells as astrocytes and microglia are involved in neuronal support, maintenance of extracellular homeostasis, and immune regulation in response to injury (Garland et al., 2022; Kwon and Koh, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garland et al., 2022; Kwon and Koh, 2020

claim: Astrocytes and microglia initially respond to injury by releasing neuroprotective neurotrophic factors and antioxidants.
source: Initially, these cells respond to injury by releasing neuroprotective neurotrophic factors and antioxidants (Garland et al., 2022; Kwon and Koh, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garland et al., 2022; Kwon and Koh, 2020

claim: Prolonged microglial activation can induce reactive astrocytes and together they release neurotoxic pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
source: However, under certain conditions, prolonged microglial activation can induce reactive astrocytes and together they release neurotoxic pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which in turn can lead to metabolic stress and foster the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau plaques in AD, ultimately contributing to heightened neuronal death (Kempuraj et al., 2016; Yun et al., 2018; Liddelow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kempuraj et al., 2016; Yun et al., 2018; Liddelow et al., 2017

claim: Prolonged microglial activation can lead to metabolic stress and foster the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau plaques in Alzheimer's disease, ultimately contributing to heightened neuronal death.
source: However, under certain conditions, prolonged microglial activation can induce reactive astrocytes and together they release neurotoxic pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which in turn can lead to metabolic stress and foster the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau plaques in AD, ultimately contributing to heightened neuronal death (Kempuraj et al., 2016; Yun et al., 2018; Liddelow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kempuraj et al., 2016; Yun et al., 2018; Liddelow et al., 2017

claim: Immune and other cell type-mediated events are a driving force behind the wide range of neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Growing evidence suggests that immune and other cell type-mediated events are a driving force behind the wide range of neurodegenerative conditions (Kempuraj et al., 2016; Maccioni et al., 2009; Zang et al., 2022; Castellani et al., 2023; Balusu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kempuraj et al., 2016; Maccioni et al., 2009; Zang et al., 2022; Castellani et al., 2023; Balusu et al., 2023

claim: Brain spatial patterns in gene expression are associated with regional vulnerability to some neurodegenerative disorders and their corresponding tissue atrophy distributions.
source: Recent studies have suggested that brain spatial patterns in gene expression are associated with regional vulnerability to some neurodegenerative disorders and their corresponding tissue atrophy distributions (Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2020; Roshchupkin et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2019; Altmann et al., 2020; Kerrebijn et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2020; Roshchupkin et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2019; Altmann et al., 2020; Kerrebijn et al., 2023

claim: A comparison of transcriptomic patterns in middle temporal gyrus across various brain diseases showed cell type expression signature unique for neurodegenerative diseases.
source: A comparison of transcriptomic patterns in middle temporal gyrus across various brain diseases showed cell type expression signature unique for neurodegenerative diseases (Zeighami et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeighami et al., 2023

claim: Single-cell transcriptomics and multiomics analyses are invariably restricted to a few isolated brain regions, usually needing to be preselected at hand for each specific disease.
source: Although single-cell transcriptomics and multiomics analyses have advanced our knowledge of cell type compositions associated with pathology in neurodegeneration (Cuevas-Diaz Duran et al., 2022; Luquez et al., 2022; Riley et al., 2014), these are invariably restricted to a few isolated brain regions, usually needing to be preselected at hand for each specific disease.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cuevas-Diaz Duran et al., 2022; Luquez et al., 2022; Riley et al., 2014

claim: No whole-brain maps for the abundance of cell populations in humans are currently available.
source: Due to the invasive nature of tissue acquisition/mapping and further technical limitations for covering extended areas (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2022), no whole-brain maps for the abundance of cell populations in humans are currently available, constraining the analysis of large-scale cellular vulnerabilities in neurological diseases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Arnatkeviciute et al., 2022

claim: The study constructed whole-brain reference maps of cellular abundance in healthy humans for six canonical cell types: neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and oligodendrocyte precursors.
source: First, we use transcriptomics, structural MRI, and advanced cell deconvolution to construct whole-brain reference maps of cellular abundance in healthy humans for six canonical cell types: neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and oligodendrocyte precursors.
evidence: This is a methodological description of what the study did

claim: The study analyzed spatial associations of each healthy level of reference canonical cell types with atrophy in 13 neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Second, we describe the spatial associations of each healthy level of reference canonical cell types with atrophy in 13 low-to-high prevalent neurodegenerative conditions, including early- and late-onset AD, genetic mutations in presenilin-1 (PS1 or PSEN1), DLB, ALS, PD, and both clinical and pathological subtypes of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD).
evidence: This is a methodological description of what the study did

claim: Non-neuronal cells express substantial vulnerability to tissue loss and spatial brain alterations in most studied neurodegenerative conditions.
source: We confirm that non-neuronal cells express substantial vulnerability to tissue loss and spatial brain alterations in most studied neurodegenerative conditions, with distinct and shared across-cell and across-disorder mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analyses

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas included high-resolution coverage of nearly the entire brain, measuring expression levels for over 20,000 genes from 3702 distinct tissue samples of six postmortem specimens.
source: This included high-resolution coverage of nearly the entire brain, measuring expression levels for over 20,000 genes from 3702 distinct tissue samples of six postmortem specimens, and detailed structural MRI data (see 'Mapping gene expression data'; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen et al., 2012

claim: Gaussian process regression allowed predicting gene expression values for unobserved regions based on the mRNA values of proximal regions.
source: Gaussian process regression allowed predicting gene expression values for unobserved regions based on the mRNA values of proximal regions.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the technique used

claim: The BRETIGEA deconvolution method accurately estimated cell proportions from bulk gene expression for six major cell types: neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
source: The deconvolution method (McKenzie et al., 2018a; Chikina et al., 2015; implemented in the BRETIGEA) accurately estimated cell proportions from bulk gene expression for six major cell types (Figure 1B): neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKenzie et al., 2018a; Chikina et al., 2015 and reference to Figure 1B

claim: Astrocytes and microglia cell occurrences presented the strongest spatial associations with atrophy in most neurodegenerative conditions.
source: As shown in Figures 2A–M–3A, astrocytes and microglia cell occurrences presented the strongest spatial associations with atrophy in most neurodegenerative conditions, particularly for EOAD, LOAD, DLB, PS1, FTLD-3RTau, FTLD-4Rtau, FTLD-TDP type A, FTLD-TDP type C, bvFTD, nfvPPA, and svPPA (all p<0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 2A-M and 3A with statistical significance p<0.001, FDR-corrected

claim: Astrocytes are involved in neuronal support, extracellular homeostasis, and inflammatory regulation in response to injury.
source: Astrocytes are involved in neuronal support, extracellular homeostasis, and inflammatory regulation in response to injury, and show high susceptibility to senescence and oxidative damage (Li et al., 2021; González-Reyes et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2021; González-Reyes et al., 2017

claim: Astrocytes show high susceptibility to senescence and oxidative damage.
source: Astrocytes are involved in neuronal support, extracellular homeostasis, and inflammatory regulation in response to injury, and show high susceptibility to senescence and oxidative damage (Li et al., 2021; González-Reyes et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2021; González-Reyes et al., 2017

claim: Astrocytes play an important role in the maintenance of the blood-brain barrier.
source: Astrocytes also play an important role in the maintenance of the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which regulates the passage of molecules, ions, and cells between the blood and the brain (Preininger and Kaufer, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Preininger and Kaufer, 2022

claim: The blood-brain barrier regulates the passage of molecules, ions, and cells between the blood and the brain.
source: Astrocytes also play an important role in the maintenance of the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which regulates the passage of molecules, ions, and cells between the blood and the brain (Preininger and Kaufer, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Preininger and Kaufer, 2022

claim: Reactive astrocytes may promote vascular inflammation in the blood-brain barrier.
source: A recent study suggested that reactive astrocytes may promote vascular inflammation in the BBB (Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2022

claim: Endothelial cells showed strong spatial associations with atrophy in almost all conditions.
source: Endothelial cells, which comprise the functional component of the BBB, also showed strong spatial associations with atrophy in almost all conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Endothelial cells regulate cerebral blood flow and deliver oxygen and nutrients to the brain.
source: Endothelial cells regulate cerebral blood flow and deliver oxygen and nutrients to the brain (Pober and Sessa, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pober and Sessa, 2007

claim: Disruption of the blood-brain barrier may allow harmful substances to enter the brain, including inflammatory molecules and toxic-aggregated proteins, ultimately exacerbating neuronal damage.
source: Disruption of the BBB may allow harmful substances to enter the brain, including inflammatory molecules and toxic-aggregated proteins, ultimately exacerbating neuronal damage (Kalaria, 1997; Salmina et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalaria, 1997; Salmina et al., 2010

claim: Reduction in cerebral blood flow and vascular dysregulation are the earliest and strongest pathological biomarkers of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Reduction in cerebral blood flow and vascular dysregulation are the earliest and strongest pathological biomarkers of LOAD, PD, and other neurodegenerative disorders (Iturria-Medina et al., 2016; Globus et al., 1985; Wolters et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iturria-Medina et al., 2016; Globus et al., 1985; Wolters et al., 2020

claim: Microglial cells are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system and key players in the pathology of neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Similar to astrocytes in their role of supporting neurons, microglial cells are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system and key players in the pathology of neurodegenerative conditions, including AD, PD, FTD, and ALS (Geloso et al., 2017; Guzman-Martinez et al., 2019; Malpetti et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geloso et al., 2017; Guzman-Martinez et al., 2019; Malpetti et al., 2021

claim: Microglial activation in prolonged neuroinflammation is of particular relevance in neurodegeneration.
source: Besides its many critical specializations, microglial activation in prolonged neuroinflammation is of particular relevance in neurodegeneration (Geloso et al., 2017; Perea et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geloso et al., 2017; Perea et al., 2018

claim: At earlier stages of Alzheimer's disease, increased population of microglia and astrocytes (microgliosis and astrogliosis) has been observed in diseased regions due to sustained cellular proliferation in response to disturbances, loss of homeostasis, or the accumulation of misfolded proteins.
source: At earlier stages of AD, increased population of microglia and astrocytes (microgliosis and astrogliosis) has been observed in diseased regions due to sustained cellular proliferation in response to disturbances, loss of homeostasis, or the accumulation of misfolded proteins (Kwon and Koh, 2020; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Vandenbark et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kwon and Koh, 2020; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Vandenbark et al., 2021

claim: Excessive proliferation may lead to the transition of homeostatic microglia to its senescent or disease-associated type via the processes mediated by TREM2-APOE signaling.
source: Excessive proliferation may lead to the transition of homeostatic microglia to its senescent or disease-associated type, also known as DAM, via the processes mediated by TREM2-APOE signaling (Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021

claim: Increased number of dystrophic microglia has been seen in multiple neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and TDP-43 encephalopathy.
source: Increased number of dystrophic microglia, a form of cellular senescence characterized as beading and fragmentation of the branches of microglia, has been seen in multiple neurodegenerative conditions such as AD, DLB, and TDP-43 encephalopathy (Streit et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Streit et al., 2020

claim: The presence of senescent microglia is believed to ultimately contribute to the failure of brain homeostasis and to clinical symptomatology.
source: The presence of senescent microglia is believed to ultimately contribute to the failure of brain homeostasis and to clinical symptomatology (Balusu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2021; Lau et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Balusu et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2021; Lau et al., 2023

claim: Oligodendrocytes associated with spatial tissue vulnerability to all conditions aside from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Oligodendrocytes also associated with spatial tissue vulnerability to all conditions aside ALS (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Oligodendrocytes are responsible for the synthesis and maintenance of myelin in the brain.
source: Oligodendrocytes are responsible for the synthesis and maintenance of myelin in the brain (Armada-Moreira et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Armada-Moreira et al., 2015

claim: Demyelination produces loss of axonal insulation, leading to neuronal dysfunctions.
source: Demyelination produces loss of axonal insulation, leading to neuronal dysfunctions (Armada-Moreira et al., 2015; Mot et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armada-Moreira et al., 2015; Mot et al., 2018

claim: Myelin dysfunction may lead to secondary inflammation and subsequent failure of microglia to clear amyloid-β deposition in Alzheimer's disease mice models.
source: Myelin dysfunction may lead to secondary inflammation and subsequent failure of microglia to clear amyloid-β deposition in AD mice models (Depp et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Depp et al., 2023

claim: Oligodendrocytes were shown to be highly genetically associated with Parkinson's disease.
source: Oligodendrocytes were shown to be highly genetically associated with PD (Bryois et al., 2020; Feleke et al., 2021; Agarwal et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bryois et al., 2020; Feleke et al., 2021; Agarwal et al., 2020

claim: Densities of oligodendrocyte precursor cells showed strong correlations with the atrophy patterns of dementia with Lewy bodies, early-onset Alzheimer's disease, presenilin-1 mutation, and FTLD-TDP type C.
source: In addition, densities of OPCs showed strong correlations with the atrophy patterns of DLB, EOAD, PS1, and FTLD-TDP type C.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analyses

claim: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells regulate neural activity and harbor immune-related and vascular-related functions.
source: OPCs regulate neural activity and harbor immune-related and vascular-related functions (Akay et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Akay et al., 2021

claim: In response to oligodendrocyte damage, oligodendrocyte precursor cells initiate their proliferation and differentiation for the purpose of repairing damaged myelin.
source: In response to oligodendrocyte damage, OPCs initiate their proliferation and differentiation for the purpose of repairing damaged myelin (Ohtomo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohtomo et al., 2018

claim: In Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the oligodendrocyte precursor cells become unable to differentiate and their numbers decrease, leading to a reduction in myelin production and subsequent neural damage.
source: In AD, PD, and ALS, the OPCs become unable to differentiate and their numbers decrease, leading to a reduction in myelin production and subsequent neural damage (Traiffort et al., 2021; Spaas et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Traiffort et al., 2021; Spaas et al., 2021

claim: Neuronal abundance distribution is associated with tissue damage in many neurodegenerative conditions.
source: We observed (Figure 3A) that neuronal abundance distribution is also associated with tissue damage in many neurodegenerative conditions.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: For amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, neuron proportions positively correlated with tissue integrity.
source: However, these associations are less strong than for other cell types, except for the ALS case (Figure 2J). For this disorder, neuron proportions positively correlated with tissue integrity (i.e., the higher the neuronal proportion, the less atrophy in a region).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2J

claim: Increased neuronal presence at brain regions may have a protective effect in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, making neuronal enriched regions less vulnerable to damage in this disorder.
source: This observation suggests that increased neuronal presence at brain regions (relative to all considered cell types) may have a protective effect in ALS, making neuronal enriched regions less vulnerable to damage in this disorder.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed positive correlation between neuron proportions and tissue integrity in ALS

claim: Particularly weak associations were observed between neuronal proportions and tissue damage in all three clinical variants of frontotemporal dementia and Parkinson's disease.
source: In addition, we observed particularly weak associations between neuronal proportions and tissue damage in all three clinical variants of FTD (bvFTD, nfvPPA, svPPA) and PD (Figure 3A), suggesting that these conditions may be primarily associated with supportive cell types (microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, respectively; Figure 2I and K–M).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figures 2I and K-M

claim: Clinical variants of frontotemporal dementia and Parkinson's disease may be primarily associated with supportive cell types (microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes).
source: In addition, we observed particularly weak associations between neuronal proportions and tissue damage in all three clinical variants of FTD (bvFTD, nfvPPA, svPPA) and PD (Figure 3A), suggesting that these conditions may be primarily associated with supportive cell types (microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, respectively; Figure 2I and K–M).
evidence: This is an inference from the weak associations between neuronal proportions and tissue damage, supported by data in Figures 3A and 2I, K-M

claim: All histologically confirmed dementia conditions formed a separate cluster in the hierarchical taxonomy dendrogram.
source: The clustergram analysis revealed distinct grouping patterns among various neurodegenerative conditions. All histologically confirmed dementia conditions formed a separate cluster.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis

claim: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease and mutations in presenilin-1 grouped together in the hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: Notably, EOAD and mutations in PS1, a prevalent cause of familial EOAD (Kelleher and Shen, 2017), grouped together.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis, with citation to Kelleher and Shen, 2017 for the relationship between PS1 and EOAD

claim: Mutations in presenilin-1 are a prevalent cause of familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease.
source: Notably, EOAD and mutations in PS1, a prevalent cause of familial EOAD (Kelleher and Shen, 2017), grouped together.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelleher and Shen, 2017

claim: Three clinical subtypes of frontotemporal dementia displayed similar patterns of cell type vulnerabilities and diverged into a discrete cluster with Parkinson's disease, separately from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and other dementia conditions.
source: Interestingly, three clinical subtypes of FTD (bvFTD, nfvPPA, and svPPA) displayed similar patterns of cell type vulnerabilities and diverged into a discrete cluster with PD, separately from ALS and other dementia conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis

claim: FTLD-associated pathologies such as TDP-43 proteinopathies and three-repeat and four-repeat tauopathies showed patterns more similar to those found in dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer's disease-related conditions rather than clinical frontotemporal dementia subtypes from a different dataset.
source: However, FTLD-associated pathologies such as TDP-43 proteinopathies (types A and C), as well as three-repeat and four-repeat tauopathies, showed patterns more similar to those found in DLB and AD-related conditions (EOAD, LOAD, PS1) rather than clinical FTD subtypes from a different dataset.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis

claim: All FTLD-related subtypes and conditions showed the strongest associations with spatial distributions of glial cells, particularly astrocytes and microglia.
source: Nonetheless, all FTLD-related subtypes and conditions showed the strongest associations with spatial distributions of glial cells, particularly astrocytes and microglia.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analyses

claim: Neurons' and oligodendrocyte precursor cells' spatial density distributions were least associated with tissue atrophy in all 13 conditions.
source: Among all cell types, neurons' and OPCs' spatial density distributions were least associated with tissue atrophy in all 13 conditions, subsequently clustering together.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis

claim: Astrocytes and microglia distributions showed the strongest associations with all neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Astrocytes and microglia distributions similarly showed the strongest associations with all neurodegenerative conditions (Figure 3B), and thus formed a separate cluster while still being related with oligodendrocytes and endothelial cells.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Astrocytes and microglia are known to be intimately related in the pathophysiological processes of neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Astrocytes and microglia are known to be intimately related in the pathophysiological processes of neurodegenerative disorders (Kwon and Koh, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwon and Koh, 2020

claim: Both astrocytes and microglia are key regulators of inflammatory responses in the central nervous system.
source: Both are key regulators of inflammatory responses in the central nervous system, and given their role in clearing misfolded proteins, dysfunctions of each of them can result in the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau (Kwon and Koh, 2020; Leyns and Holtzman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kwon and Koh, 2020; Leyns and Holtzman, 2017

claim: Dysfunctions of astrocytes and microglia can result in the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau.
source: Both are key regulators of inflammatory responses in the central nervous system, and given their role in clearing misfolded proteins, dysfunctions of each of them can result in the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau (Kwon and Koh, 2020; Leyns and Holtzman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kwon and Koh, 2020; Leyns and Holtzman, 2017

claim: During the progression of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, microglia's activation can result in an increased capacity to convert resting astrocytes to reactive astrocytes.
source: During the progression of AD and PD, microglia's activation can result in an increased capacity to convert resting astrocytes to reactive astrocytes (Liddelow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liddelow et al., 2017

claim: Patterns in cellular vulnerability in dementia with Lewy bodies did not strongly resemble Parkinson's disease without dementia.
source: Patterns in cellular vulnerability in DLB did not strongly resemble PD without dementia (Figure 3C), although both conditions involve alpha-synuclein aggregates (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and citation to Kim et al., 2014

claim: Both dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease involve alpha-synuclein aggregates.
source: Patterns in cellular vulnerability in DLB did not strongly resemble PD without dementia (Figure 3C), although both conditions involve alpha-synuclein aggregates (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2014

claim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis did not group together with frontotemporal dementia variants and FTLD-associated pathologies based on patterns of cell-atrophy associations.
source: A similar observation can be made for ALS and FTLD. Despite the common presence of TDP-43 abnormal accumulations and their strong genetical overlap (Ferrari et al., 2011), ALS did not group together with FTD variants and FTLD-associated pathologies based on patterns of cell–atrophy associations.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis, with citation to Ferrari et al., 2011

claim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal lobar degeneration have common presence of TDP-43 abnormal accumulations and strong genetical overlap.
source: A similar observation can be made for ALS and FTLD. Despite the common presence of TDP-43 abnormal accumulations and their strong genetical overlap (Ferrari et al., 2011), ALS did not group together with FTD variants and FTLD-associated pathologies based on patterns of cell–atrophy associations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferrari et al., 2011

claim: TDP-43 is the usual cause of semantic variant primary progressive aphasia and approximately half of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia cases.
source: All these conditions are known to be pathologically linked, often arising from either tau or TDP-43 accumulation; for instance, TDP-43 is the usual cause of svPPA and approximately half of bvFTD cases, while the other half of bvFTD patients and many nfvPPA cases are associated with tau pathology (Perry and Miller, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry and Miller, 2013

claim: The other half of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia patients and many non-fluent variant primary progressive aphasia cases are associated with tau pathology.
source: All these conditions are known to be pathologically linked, often arising from either tau or TDP-43 accumulation; for instance, TDP-43 is the usual cause of svPPA and approximately half of bvFTD cases, while the other half of bvFTD patients and many nfvPPA cases are associated with tau pathology (Perry and Miller, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perry and Miller, 2013

claim: Network topology and other factors beyond the presence of toxic misfolded proteins play a fundamental role in developing characteristic tissue loss and cellular vulnerability in neurodegenerative conditions.
source: These results emphasize the fundamental role of network topology and other factors beyond the presence of toxic misfolded proteins in developing characteristic tissue loss and cellular vulnerability in neurodegenerative conditions (Zeighami et al., 2015; Iturria-Medina and Evans, 2015; Tremblay et al., 2021; Zeighami et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed dissimilarities between conditions with similar protein pathologies, supported by citations to Zeighami et al., 2015; Iturria-Medina and Evans, 2015; Tremblay et al., 2021; Zeighami et al., 2019

claim: The study characterized large-scale spatial associations between canonical cell types and brain tissue loss across cortical and subcortical gray matter areas in 13 neurodegenerative conditions.
source: In the most systematic study of its kind, here we characterized large-scale spatial associations between canonical cell types and brain tissue loss across cortical and subcortical GM areas in 13 neurodegenerative conditions (including EOAD, LOAD, PD, DLB, ALS, mutations in PS1, and clinical [bvFTD, nfvPPA, svPPA] and pathological [three-repeat and four-repeat tauopathies and TDPP43 proteinopathies types A and C] subtypes of FTLD).
evidence: This is a description of what the study did

claim: The study derived high-resolution maps of cellular abundance/proportion in the adult human healthy brain for six canonical cell types, including astrocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and endothelial cells.
source: We derived, first to our knowledge, high-resolution maps of cellular abundance/proportion in the adult human healthy brain for six canonical cell types, including astrocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a description of what the study did

claim: Previous cellular analyses of neurological conditions have been restricted to expert-selected isolated brain areas.
source: As mentioned, previous cellular analyses of neurological conditions have been restricted to expert-selected isolated brain areas.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research

claim: The invasive nature of expression assays, requiring direct access to neural tissue, and other numerous scaling limitations have impeded extensive spatial analyses.
source: The invasive nature of expression assays, requiring direct access to neural tissue, and other numerous scaling limitations have impeded extensive spatial analyses (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019

claim: Many neurodegeneration-related genes have similar levels of expression in both affected and unaffected brain areas.
source: Since many neurodegeneration-related genes have similar levels of expression in both affected and unaffected brain areas (Jackson, 2014), characterizing changes in tissue loss associated with reference cell type proportions in health may provide a clearer perspective on large-scale spatial patterns of cellular vulnerability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jackson, 2014

claim: All canonical cell types express vulnerability to dementia-related atrophy of brain tissue.
source: Our results demonstrate that all canonical cell types express vulnerability to dementia-related atrophy of brain tissue, potentially suggesting the disruption of the molecular pathways involving specific cell types can contribute to their observed dysfunctions and subsequent clinical symptomatology (Balusu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analyses, with citation to Balusu et al., 2023

claim: Transcriptional profiling of prefrontal cortex in Alzheimer's disease showed reduced proportions of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and homeostatic microglia.
source: Previously, transcriptional profiling of prefrontal cortex in AD showed reduced proportions of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and homeostatic microglia (Lau et al., 2020).
